newsitem.title: FRANCE: Apple denies Pippin decision made yet.
newsitem.headline: Apple denies Pippin decision made yet.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc unveiled two new products on Tuesday at the MILIA multimedia fair and denied rumours that it had already decided to scrap the Pippin multimedia and game station.

"We have not yet decided. We will honour our commitments to our licence holders," Bjoern Gustavsson, general manager Europe of Apple's Performa & Information Appliance Division, said about Pippin at a news conference.
The troubled computer maker is undergoing a major restructuring and speculation is growing over the future of Pippin, including that it might be sold.
Japan's Bandai, which recently struck an alliance deal with computer game giant Sega, has a licence for the Pippin and Katz Media will shortly launch the CD-ROM game player in France.
"I believe that a machine like the Pippin can help get the necessary volumes for CD-ROM publishers to finally make some money," Gustavsson added.
He also unveiled the "eMate" portable computer for schoolchildren, due to be sold at $700 in the United States, with shipping scheduled for March.
The eMate is a sturdy but light computer tailored for the school environment, using the platform of the Newton digital assistant. It will be launched in Europe later.
Gustavsson was standing in for Apple chief operating officer Marco Landi who could not come to Europe due to the Cupertino-based computer group's latest restructuring.
He displayed a product with the code name "Hooper" which will be launched next month.

Hooper is a powerbook portable computer with a PowerPC chip at more than 200 Megaherz speed, allowing a realistic video image which was demonstrated with a little camera mounted on top of the machine, carried around the conference room.
"We broke the 200Mhz barrier for laptops," Gustavsson said.
Apple also unveiled the sleek "Spartacus" concept computer which marries modern design with high technological performance and a Bose sound system.

Giving a broad overview of Apple's performance, Gustavsson noted special charges had been taken in the last quarter due to disappointing Christmas sales in the United States. But he noted high demand for Internet servers.
"We are now in the phase of cleaning up the house," he said, adding that in phase two there would be clear responsibility, accountability and measurability within Apple.
The third stage would see a further simplification of manufacturing, using a "lego" system of plug-and-play common components to roll out the various Apple products.

Apple is committed to releasing a major upgrade of its MacOS operating system every six months, while developing the Rhapsody new operating system with Steve Jobs' Next. Rhapsody promises to be compatible with the old MacOS as well as having an open standard for other applications.
"We will have to be able to run Windows applications on Mac," Gustavsson said.

Apple remains bullish despite its financial problems and the many obstacles for the PowerPC chip consortium to make major inroads in the computer market dominated by the "Wintel" duo of Microsoft's Windows and Intel chips.

Gustavsson said Apple dominated the Publishing and New Media markets, with 85 percent of digital media content being developed with MacOS and 64 percent of pages on the world wide web created with Apple systems.
